cialdini-persuasion.title: Give the reader reasons to trust
cialdini-persuasion.author: Robert Cialdini
cialdini-persuasion.summary: Use relevant social proof, expertise and real terms to help the reader assess the offer.
cialdini-persuasion.useWhen: When customers are unsure who you are, whether the solution fits or whether others have benefited.
cialdini-persuasion.avoidWhen: When you lack evidence for testimonials, credentials, limitations or a claimed shared identity.
principles: Reciprocity: give something useful without a hidden obligation. Scarcity: describe only real limitations.
Authority: show relevant expertise. Consistency: make a voluntary next step easier.
Liking: write with warmth and attention. Social proof: use relevant customer examples with permission.
Unity: draw on an actual shared identity. Choose what helps the decision; do not force every principle into the copy.
questions: Which doubt should the evidence address?
Is the example relevant to this customer?
Do we have a source, permission and the right context?

example.context: Fictional: three small accounting firms have approved interviews about how they use the service.
example.before: The obvious choice for every successful firm.
example.after: Read how three small accounting firms use the service in their daily work.
example.explanation: Show the evidence so readers can assess it for themselves.

copy-structure.title: Put the argument in a clear order
copy-structure.author: Copyhackers / established writing models
copy-structure.summary: Use AIDA, PAS or before–after–bridge to organise copy once the facts and main argument are clear.
copy-structure.useWhen: When the material is useful but the reader gets it in the wrong order.
copy-structure.avoidWhen: When the structure encourages exaggeration, manufactured problems or filler. Choose a form that fits the length.
principles: AIDA: earn relevant attention, develop interest, show a desirable benefit and make the next action clear.
PAS: describe a known problem, explain its actual consequences and show the solution. Do not amplify worry without evidence.
Before–after–bridge: show a possible change and how the service helps. The future scenario must be reasonable.
questions: What does the reader need to understand first?
Is there a clear connection between the problem, offer and action?

example.context: Fictional: a service displays the team's tasks in a shared list.
example.before: Total control. Maximum potential. Unlimited possibilities.
example.after: Hard to see what's left to do? Put your tasks in one shared list. See how it works.
example.explanation: A simple sequence is enough. This example does not demonstrate a conversion improvement.

dunford-positioning.title: Make the difference matter
dunford-positioning.author: April Dunford
dunford-positioning.summary: Start with the customer's real alternatives and explain which differences matter to the right buyer.
dunford-positioning.useWhen: When readers do not understand what the product is, who it suits or why they should choose it.
dunford-positioning.avoidWhen: When the differences are generic words such as innovative, seamless or leading.
principles: Find out what customers would do without the product, including manual work or doing nothing.
Connect actual features to concrete benefits and the customers who value them.
Choose a category that helps customers understand the offer. Do not claim uniqueness without a comparison.
questions: What does the service replace today?
Which difference can we demonstrate?
Who benefits most from that difference?

example.context: Fictional: a scheduling tool collects shifts and lets staff request swaps. The customer's alternative is a spreadsheet and email.
example.before: An innovative platform that takes your business to the next level.
example.after: Keep the rota and shift-swap requests in one place.
example.explanation: Describe the relevant change in the work.

fogg-action.title: Make the next step possible
fogg-action.author: BJ Fogg
fogg-action.summary: Assess whether readers want to act, can do so without unnecessary friction and receive a clear prompt at the right time.
fogg-action.useWhen: When readers seem interested but get stuck at a form, booking or next step.
fogg-action.avoidWhen: When the problem needs a product change: describe it separately rather than promising a new button label will solve it.
principles: Consider motivation, ability and the prompt together.
Explain what the action involves and what happens afterwards.
Separate problems copy can solve from unnecessary steps that need changing in the service.
questions: Does the reader understand what the button does?
Which information is actually needed now?
Is the next step reasonable in this situation?

example.context: Fictional: the form sends a request for a quote. It does not place an order.
example.explanation: The button says what happens. Only add terms about commitments when they are known.

hopkins-testing.title: Test the message in the real world
hopkins-testing.author: Claude Hopkins / our application for evaluation
hopkins-testing.summary: State a clear hypothesis and distinguish what you expect to work from what a relevant measurement actually shows.
hopkins-testing.useWhen: When choosing between messages or finding out whether a change helps the reader and the business.
hopkins-testing.avoidWhen: When the sample is too small or the measurement confounds traffic, audiences and other changes.
principles: Write down what you are changing, why, for whom and which outcome you want to see.
Check clarity and accuracy before measuring effects.
Your own assessment or a small sample is not a measured conversion gain. Report uncertain results as uncertain.
questions: What is the hypothesis?
What counts as a relevant outcome?
Can the measurement separate the copy's effect from other changes?

example.context: Fictional: two headlines are candidates for a test. Neither has been tested yet.
example.before: The new headline will increase conversion.
example.after: Hypothesis: a headline that explains what's included makes the offer easier to understand.
example.explanation: State what you want to investigate. The modern measurement advice here is our application, not quotations from Hopkins.

hormozi-offer.title: Make the offer easy to assess
hormozi-offer.author: Alex Hormozi
hormozi-offer.summary: Clarify the benefit, why customers can believe in it, how long it takes and what they need to do themselves.
hormozi-offer.useWhen: When the price feels high, the value is unclear or the offer asks too much of the buyer.
hormozi-offer.avoidWhen: When you only need to correct a sentence. A value equation cannot guarantee prices or sales forecasts.
principles: Start with the result the customer wants and the part you can actually deliver.
Show relevant evidence and how you work. Stronger language does not replace proof.
Distinguish the start, the first benefit and the final result. Be clear about the customer's own effort.
Bonuses should address a real obstacle. Guarantees, discounts and deadlines need actual terms.
questions: What exactly does the customer get for the price?
What makes the buyer uncertain?
Which effort and waiting time can you actually reduce?

example.context: Fictional: an accounting firm handles ongoing bookkeeping, offers an introductory call and answers emails on weekdays.
example.before: Unlock your financial potential with our irresistible solution.
example.after: We handle your day-to-day bookkeeping. You get an introductory call and can email us when you need help.
example.explanation: Specify the service and support without promising a financial result.

jobs-to-be-done.title: Understand why the customer wants to switch
jobs-to-be-done.author: Christensen Institute / Jobs to Be Done
jobs-to-be-done.summary: Investigate the situation that makes someone seek a solution, the change they want and what holds them back.
jobs-to-be-done.useWhen: When the audience is described only by age, industry or company size, or when buyers hesitate to switch.
jobs-to-be-done.avoidWhen: When you have no interviews: write questions and hypotheses, not claims about what customers really feel.
principles: Ask about a specific occasion: what happened, what did the customer try and why did it matter then?
Distinguish practical value, social context and emotional needs.
Describe both the reason to switch and the obstacle. One customer's story is not a fact about the whole audience.
questions: What triggered the search?
What works poorly with the current alternative?
What would make switching difficult or uncertain?

example.context: Fictional: a service helps small businesses move bookkeeping records from another system. This is not based on a real interview.
example.before: Our solution suits businesses with 1–10 employees.
example.after: Switching accounting systems? We help you move your records from the one you use today.
example.explanation: A relevant situation can say more than a demographic description.

ogilvy-headline.title: Give the headline a clear idea
ogilvy-headline.author: David Ogilvy / our application
ogilvy-headline.summary: Understand the product and the reader. Then choose a headline that says something meaningful and that the rest of the copy can support.
ogilvy-headline.useWhen: When the headline is interchangeable, overloaded or promises more than the page shows.
ogilvy-headline.avoidWhen: When a general headline rule is treated as a guarantee of results.
principles: Build the headline's idea from real product and customer knowledge.
Show specific supporting evidence in the body copy.
Check that the wording sounds like the brand and works in the chosen channel.
questions: What does the reader learn from the headline alone?
Where on the page do we support the promise?

example.context: Fictional: customers can choose a delivery window, but no exact delivery time is guaranteed.
example.before: Delivery exactly when you want it. Every time.
example.after: Choose a delivery window that suits you.
example.explanation: Preserve the actual choice without turning it into a stronger guarantee.

schwartz-awareness.title: Start where the reader is
schwartz-awareness.author: Eugene Schwartz
schwartz-awareness.summary: Adapt the opening to what the reader already knows about the problem, the available solutions and the product.
schwartz-awareness.useWhen: When copy explains the obvious or asks for a purchase before the reader understands the offer.
schwartz-awareness.avoidWhen: When awareness is only a guess: treat the level as a hypothesis and try alternatives.
principles: Distinguish readers who have not noticed the problem, know the problem, compare solutions, know the product or already consider the offer.
A new visitor may need context. A buyer comparing options needs differences, terms and evidence.
Start with the channel and situation. The same person may know different amounts in different contexts.
questions: What does the reader already know?
Which question needs answering before the next step feels reasonable?

example.context: Fictional: the reader is comparing removal firms. The page lets them send the same enquiry to three companies.
example.before: Moving means changing where you live.
example.after: Ask three removal firms for a quote with one enquiry.
example.explanation: For a reader comparing options, the service's function may be a better opening than explaining a familiar problem.

swedish-original.title: Write as if the idea began in Swedish
swedish-original.author: Isof / our Swedish writing guide
swedish-original.summary: Start with the reader's situation and the brand's voice. Write natural Swedish with concrete words, idiomatic sentence structure and clear actions.
swedish-original.useWhen: When Swedish copy sounds translated, impersonal or full of anglicisms and sweeping sales promises.
swedish-original.avoidWhen: When an expressive voice is deliberately right for the brand. Swedish copy need not be restrained, stiff or the same for everyone.
principles: Write directly in Swedish from the facts and purpose. Keep the message but rebuild sentences when English dictates the rhythm.
Choose forms of address and technical terms for the reader. Do not assume every Swedish audience wants the same tone.
Describe actions and benefits specifically. Keep humour, emotion and energy when they help.
Check compound words, headings, currency, units and dates. Do not change the offer's facts or terms to fit the language.
questions: Would someone in this audience say it this way?
What does the wording mean in practice?
Does it sound like this brand rather than a translated template?

example.context: Fictional: a subscription tool displays recurring costs. Savings are not guaranteed. The wording below shows the same contrast in English; this framework is specifically about Swedish copy.
example.before: Unlock savings and take control of your financial journey.
example.after: See what your subscriptions cost each month.
example.explanation: This example is our own application. Isof's plain-language guidance supports clarity, not claims about sales performance.

wiebe-customer-language.title: Find the words in the customer's everyday life
wiebe-customer-language.author: Joanna Wiebe / Copyhackers
wiebe-customer-language.summary: Collect customers' questions, objections and descriptions of the problem before choosing the message.
wiebe-customer-language.useWhen: When the copy relies on internal product terms or you need to understand what buyers want to know.
wiebe-customer-language.avoidWhen: When there are no customer sources: do not invent quotations or call your assumptions customer insight.
principles: Read interviews, support questions and reviews you are allowed to use, keeping their context.
Distinguish quotations, paraphrases and your own interpretation. Record the source and the limits of the sample.
Check whether people understand the message. Let customer language inform the copy without erasing the brand's voice.
questions: Which questions recur?
How does the customer describe the problem before knowing the product?
What needs to be checked with more people?

example.context: Fictional: the service collects receipts. In an invented customer conversation, a business owner describes searching for them before doing the books.
example.after: Keep receipts in one place, so you can find them when it's time to do the books.
example.explanation: Choose concrete words and a recognisable situation.
